In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''secant variety''' <math>\operatorname{Sect}(V)</math>, or the '''variety of chords''', of a [[projective variety]] <math>V \subset \mathbb{P}^r</math> is the [[Zariski closure]] of the union of all [[secant line]]s (chords) to ''V'' in <math>\mathbb{P}^r</math>:<ref>{{harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|loc=pg. 173}}</ref>
:<math>\operatorname{Sect}(V) = \bigcup_{x, y \in V} \overline{xy}</math>
(for <math>x = y</math>, the line <math>\overline{xy}</math> is the [[tangent line]].) It is also the image under the projection <math>p_3: (\mathbb{P}^r)^3 \to \mathbb{P}^r</math> of the closure ''Z'' of the [[incidence variety]]
:<math>\{ (x, y, l) | x \wedge y \wedge l = 0 \}</math>.
Note that ''Z'' has dimension <math>2 \dim V + 1</math> and so <math>\operatorname{Sect}(V)</math> has dimension at most <math>2 \dim V + 1</math>.

More generally, the '''<math>k^{th}</math> secant variety''' is the Zariski closure of the union of the linear spaces spanned by collections of ''k''+1 points on <math>V</math>. It may be denoted by <math>\Sigma_k</math>. The above secant variety is the first secant variety.  Unless <math>\Sigma_k=\mathbb{P}^r</math>, it is always [[Singular point of an algebraic variety|singular]] along <math>\Sigma_{k-1}</math>, but may have other singular points.

If <math>V</math> has dimension ''d'', the dimension of <math>\Sigma_k</math> is at most <math>kd+d+k</math>.
A useful tool for computing the dimension of a secant variety is [[Terracini's lemma]].

== Examples ==
A secant variety can be used to show the fact that a [[smooth variety|smooth]] [[projective curve]] can be embedded into the projective 3-space <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math> as follows.<ref>{{harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|loc=pg. 215}}</ref> Let <math>C \subset \mathbb{P}^r</math> be a smooth curve. Since the dimension of the secant variety ''S'' to ''C'' has dimension at most 3, if <math>r > 3</math>, then there is a point ''p'' on <math>\mathbb{P}^r</math> that is not on ''S'' and so we have the [[projection from a point|projection]] <math>\pi_p</math> from ''p'' to a hyperplane ''H'', which gives the embedding <math>\pi_p: C \hookrightarrow H \simeq \mathbb{P}^{r-1}</math>. Now repeat.

If <math>S \subset \mathbb{P}^5</math> is a surface that does not lie in a [[hyperplane]] and if <math>\operatorname{Sect}(S) \ne \mathbb{P}^5</math>, then ''S'' is a [[Veronese surface]].<ref>{{harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|loc=pg. 179}}</ref>
